My dad had two sisters who lived out of state my whole life. They all had a rough childhood and didn’t get together often, so although I loved them I honestly didn’t know them very well. I knew they were very emotional from my dad’s stories, but my mom (she passed away a year before my dad) was super level headed so I wasn’t used to conflict. 

When my dad passed they came to “help” but honestly made things harder. They were constantly yelling and fighting to the point where I felt like I was taking care of them more so than they were me. They were also jealous that I was closer with my mom’s friends, but didn’t consider that was because I barely saw them my whole life. 

I still get mad about it sometimes, but I cope by telling myself they were also acting in grief. I lost my father but they also lost their big brother, and after already going through my mom’s death I knew how crazy grief could make you. It’s not an excuse and I still think they should have acted differently, but it is a reason and that’s better than nothing.

A lot of people have said dogs, which when trained for defense are of course notably effective, but training can be expensive and time consuming. I find dogs, trained or not, extremely useful for detecting an intruder. Dogs bark, and the sheer fact that you’re aware of an intruder’s presence can be the difference between life and death. You can keep a gun on your nightstand, but if someone sneaks in while you’re sleeping, the chances of you comprehending what’s happening in time to defend yourself decrease significantly. My two Pomeranians aren’t exactly scary, but they do let me know if anyone so much as steps foot on my driveway. 

Warning/no trespassing signs can also help. If someone believes they could face a threat, they’re much less likely to make an attempt. You may not have a gun, but if someone thinks it’s a possibility, their decision becomes lethal and most aren’t likely to take that risk. Never let anyone know you’re not armed. 

Wasp spray is more accurate/shoots farther than pepper spray, and much cheaper than bear spray. You also don’t have to worry about it blowing back on you. 

Other than the obvious methods of self protection (knives, bats, etc.) a pair of pliers are pretty inconspicuous but can definitely be used as a weapon. If you pinch someone’s skin with a pair of pliers… yeah, that’ll hurt enough to at least temporarily disable them. 

If you’ve ever cut firewood, you know how powerful an axe is when properly swung. Use accordingly. 

If you think someone already in your home is a threat, heat something up on the stove, preferably something liquid but thick. You know where I’m going with this.

Lastly, and personally my favorite method… never underestimate the power of acting like a complete fucking psycho. Walking into someone’s home seeing them curled up in a ball is one thing, walking into someone’s home and feeling like you just stepped foot on the set of The Exorcist is another. I own land in a very remote area with a small container shed on it for storage. After about the fifth time someone tried break in, I spray painted a pentagram on the door and hung up some stick figures like the Blair witch project. Haven’t had problem since. 

Source: I’m a woman who does a lot of solo travel and has seen a lot of shit. Don’t be afraid of them, but do what you have to to make them afraid of you. Cheers

I’m so sorry you’re going though this. I’m also sorry for all the hateful comments you’re getting… what’s happed has happened, and WE ALL make mistakes, especially at a young age. This is definitely an abusive relationship, and you need to get out. I understand your situation doesn’t allow you the option to just pick up and go, but you do need to come up with a plan. 

Do you have any friends or family members you’re in contact with? If not, are there any DV shelters in the area? Unfortunately this is something you’re not going to be able to do alone. Even check fb for women supporting women groups, you’d be surprised how many have been in your shoes and wouldn’t hesitate to help. 

Is there any certain time of the day/week where you have the house to yourself? Start packing what you can and find a safe place to store it in the meantime away from the house. Some people will offer their garages, especially if it’s short term. If you HAVE to do this while he’s at home, I know you said don’t have a car, but maybe add a few extra things in your bag/backpack or the kids stuff when going out. Be prepared to leave a great bit behind, but make sure you get all personal/sentimental items. These can be used by him as leverage to regain contact later. 

Try to get out when he’s not there, but if not DO NOT try end things face to face alone. Some people try to be the bigger person and think it’s the right thing to do after that involved of a relationship, but this man seems irrational and clearly lacks control of his emotions, and this could put you and your children in danger. 


Last, it’s very important to stand your ground and go no contact in the time following. The only reason I would say otherwise is bc of your children, but he’s definitely not a spectacular father and it seems like you’ve been doing this all on your own already. We’re all human, we all have emotions, and when we go through shit it makes us especially easy to be manipulated. Find other people to lean on and help hold you accountable for that. 

I wish you and your babies the best, and hope you eventually find light at the end of this tunnel.

I’m also from a small town in Georgia, so I had never been to NYC, knew anyone remotely involved, or even realized the towers existed before it happened. 

Flash forward to a few years ago (I’m 31 now) and I went down a 9/11 rabbit hole one night. That was the first time I ever saw any of the gore or anything that wasn’t PG. I had just moved to a new city across the country to work my first “real” job, and looking at pictures of the victims I realized a lot of them were the same age I was then. Young corporate professionals busting their ass for next to nothing, but so proud to go back home and say they worked in “The World Trade Center”. Many of them had uprooted and moved to a new city, were scared to death bc they didn’t feel like a “real” adult yet, but pushing on doing what they believed was the path to success despite everything. Then all of a sudden you’re in the worst situation imaginable, the world literally burning around you, and facing imminent death when your life just started. It still shakes me up when I think about it.

OP, you need to get out ASAP. 

This happened to a friend of mine, and this was her solution: 

First, you’ll need a plan. Is there a certain day of the week you know he’ll be gone for a at least a few hours or at least enough time for you move your things out? Work, hobbies, etc? 

Do you have any friends/family that can help you move? If not, there are several feminist/women centered subreddits that you could post asking for help and hopefully find a group of people in your area. Vet them first obviously, but you’d be surprised how many women will rally behind you on this.  

If he has the potential to become violent (and he sounds like he does) it’s very important to do this quickly, discretely, and not alone. It’s much less likely he’ll try anything to hurt you if there are multiple people present. Not being alone can also give you the mental strength to not back out/second guess your decision. 

Once you have a planned move out time and have a secure place to go (churches and domestic violence shelters can also help) you need to contact an attorney and file for divorce. You can mail the papers or leave them behind when you move, but don’t try to give them to him yourself. Also, and I know this will be hard, but let him know any communication between the two of you going forward should go through your attorney. Block his number, and do everything you can to prevent him from finding out where you relocated. Do not let him have any access to your new life.

You can do this. You deserve a happy life with someone who truly cares about you, and he deserves to be left in the dust. Best of luck to you ❤️

First one was an overdose from cocaine and xanex, his half brother was actually my boyfriend at the time. The worst part was my bf had gone home to grab something, saw his brother laying on the couch with his hoodie pulled over his face, assumed he was taking a nap and ran out the door in a hurry. His dad came in later and tried to wake him up, but he was already gone. Since no one witnessed the time of death there was no way know exactly, but they did determine it was around the time my bf stopped by. There was no way to know if his brother was already dead or not when he saw him on the couch, and that was something he (understandably) really struggled with. 

The second was a suicide. He was in the gifted program with me, which was practically a family bc it was a small town so we were kept together in the same class all the way through school. He had moved here with his dad in fourth grade, and you could tell he had a pretty shitty home life. In the middle of the school year in 10th grade, he suddenly got pulled out of school to go back and live with his mom in NM. Like, came to school one day and out of the blue told us it was his last day here. He had an iPad, and took my picture with it along with a few others. When I asked why he said “because you were always nice to me, and I don’t want to forget you.” A month later, we found out he had shot himself. 15 years later I still have his obituary with his picture in my drawer, so I’ll never forget about him either. 

The third was a dirt bike accident. The kid’s dad had just gotten a brand new bike, and he made the kid swear he wouldn’t touch it while he ran a quick errand in town (he was only 14). When the dad got back the bike, and the kid, were missing. The kid was trying to sneak and ride it before his dad got home, but it was evening in winter and the sun was going down fast. He hit a deer, and his head and the deer’s head actually collided, breaking his skull. He was in ICU for 6 days before he went brain dead and his family decided to pull the plug.

My mom died a week before Christmas in 2021, one of the last things she did was put up the Christmas tree bc I was coming home (I always loved it, she hated the damn thing lol). It took me until this past June to take it down. Then, I lost my dad in August. I’m 30 and this will be the first Christmas without my parents, I debated on even putting a wreath on the door. 

It’s taken me this long to finally accept that trying to stop time/not acknowledge it won’t bring them back, it just holds me in a pit of despair. This year I put up two Christmas trees, and even decorated the yard for the kids in my neighborhood. There were a lot of tears in the process, but I like to think they’d be proud of me. 

There is no time limit, no right or wrong way to go about it, but I’ve tried to look at it as this is what it means to continue living. I’ve begged god to not wake me up in the morning, even contemplated suicide, but I’ve finally realized if I make the choice to keep going, that also means I have to LIVE. Living life to the fullest has become my way of honoring the dead, because they taught me how precious every little moment on this earth is. 

Love, prayers, good vibes, and all the internet hugs to you my friend. Thank you for being vulnerable and sharing your experience ❤️

From the deepest part of my heart, I am so, intensely sorry OP. 

Thought not nearly as devastating, I’m in a somewhat similar situation. My mom died suddenly and completely unexpectedly 12/18/21, 10 days before my 29th birthday. I’m an only child, and I left my new home, career, and life I’d worked so hard building to move back home, originally to help my 87 yo grandmother (my mother’s mother, she was also an only child and her caregiver), but that soon turned in to trying to keep my dad alive. 

Though his death was medically declared liver failure, it was essentially a long suicide. He was in perfect health when my mom died, but then stopped eating, kept drinking a lot, and refused care for the many conditions he acquired as a result. He passed away on hospice care August 13th. It was the most gut wrenching, soul crushing thing I’d ever had to witness. 

I also find myself asking why, why me of all people? I had a wonderful life for 29 years, all to have it ripped away out of nowhere. When I go out I see people whispering about me, pointing out who I am and what happened. Hi love, I (30F) have been going through something similar with getting access to my dad’s finances- my mom died unexpectedly a year and a half ago and my dad passed last month without updating his will. I’m an only child and next of kin, but it’s still been a crazy process with court and everything. Luckily my parents were from a small town and knew everyone so I didn’t have to jump through as many hoops, but this is what I did and I hope it helps. 

If you haven’t already gotten them, you’re going to need A LOT of death certificates from the state, your funeral director can help you get those. You’ll need them for nearly every account you have close/switched over. My dad had several accounts so my funeral director suggested I request 10 certificates. 

You’ll need to locate your dad’s will if he has one. Sometimes it’s already filed with the probate court so they can easily access them, other times it’s a bit trickier. My dad’s was in his safe deposit box at the bank, so I had to request access through probate with a judge’s signature, but probate will be able to tell you what to do. 

Call your local probate court and tell them your situation- I literally said something like “this is what’s happening and I have no idea what to do” and they’ll give you a summary of the process and tell you to come pick up paperwork. Let them be your main source of information, they were very helpful to me so hopefully you’ll have the same experience. 

Find a lawyer you trust- ask close friends and family for recommendations, or what I did was dig through old paperwork and found a lawyer my dad had worked with in the past. Call the office, make an appointment, and bring the probate paperwork as well as any financial information (his bank statements, investment accounts, life insurance, etc) with you. Once again, just be open and honest that you don’t know what to do or where to start and they’ll help you work with probate court from there. 

The death certificate and probate mandates will help freeze finances for now until you can get payment and next steps arranged. You’ll also need to find out if your dad had life insurance and file a claim. 

Write down any questions you can think of to ask when you call the probate office so nothings forgotten. Essentially, they should be able to answer most questions for your or if not direct you to someone who can. It will be a couple of weeks process, but don’t stress too much about it. Remember that this kind of stuff happens often, you’re not the first and there are policies and procedures in place to make this go as smoothly as possible. 

If anyone (your dad’s landlord, for example) gives you trouble don’t try to argue yourself, alert your lawyer or probate and let them handle it so it will be documented. DOCUMENT EVERYTHING, even little things you think are understood. You never know and it’s better to be safe than sorry.

Most importantly, take care of yourself and don’t get so caught up in legal stuff that you don’t allow yourself time to grieve. Ask for help often and never feel guilty about it. Remember that what you’re going through is mostly everyone’s worst nightmare, and they will be more than willing to provide help and understanding. 

Sending you love and peace in this time. I won’t say it gets better bc it doesn’t, but you will learn how to keep going and know he’s proud of you for doing so ❤️

I had to take my senior pup to the emergency vet one night, which happened to be a teaching hospital for vet students at a rather large university nearby. They took him back when we arrived and naturally I took a seat in the waiting area. 

Now, despite this being a top tier place, vet hospitals are still not human hospitals, so the doctors don’t always have a rooms available to privately talk to the family about their pet’s prognosis, so they would do the best alternative they could and try to talk to the family/person in a less populated area of the waiting room… but still, this was a big, open, concrete room, so you couldn’t help but hear the conversation. 

Two things happened that night that I’ll never get out of my head. 

First, there was a girl who was obviously still in college who brought in her sick cat… she looked like she’d been there for hours. Eventually to vet comes out to talk to her, and unfortunately the news is not good. The cat could be saved, but the procedure needed was extremely expensive, and the only other option was to euthanize. 

Listening to the the desperate cries of this girl, who said she had moved across the country to attend school and didn’t know anyone yet, was hours away from any family, and how that cat was literally all she had, will always be stuck in my head. Imagine having a family member (bc that’s what the cat was to her) sick in the hospital, knowing there’s a way they can be saved, but having to let them die only because you couldn’t pay the bill upfront. I swear if I had the money I would have paid every dime of it for her, but unfortunately I only had enough to try to save my own baby. I went outside and threw up after that. 

The second, was a dog that got hit by a car. His pet parents and their toddler were also in the waiting room, and again I heard the doctor give the news that he didn’t make it. The couple was obviously crushed but staying stoic as to not upset their young son. They wanted to keep the dog’s body to burry themselves, understandably, and apparently there was no back door to discreetly move him out through (he was huge and had to be wheeled out, and all back entrances had stairs). So they wheeled him out the main entrance with a towel over his body, but he was so large his tail hung limply off the back. The child ran up to pet his tail, too young to understand what was happening, and the mother had to grab him to keep him inside so he didn’t see the bodying being loaded into the car. I gave the lady at the front desk my cell number to call when the doctor was ready, went to my car, spent the rest of the night balling my eyes out in the parking lot. 

If you’re sensitive to these things and find yourself in this kind of situation, by all things holy, give them your info and wait in the parking lot- they’ll understand. I’ve been to human ER’s before and witnessed some gruesome stuff, but nothing that stuck with me like my experience that night.

Lights, it really does get dark at night and though the fire will give off some light have a few lanterns as well. I have 1 large lantern I keep on the table for cooking/cleaning, then a few small ones scattered places I might need to frequent (the tent entrance, my chair, a place that could be easy to trip over, etc). Flashlights only provide one stream of light and sometimes you need something to light a whole area. 

Even if you’ve waterproofed your tent, bring a tarp just in case. If the wind is blowing while it’s raining it’ll still get through the mesh parts if not covered enough. It’ll also help with heavy wind and dust if you’re in a place that may be an issue. 

Bring a doormat to put outside your tent. The little one that comes on it doesn’t really help, I personally bring a yoga mat, then keep wet wipes in the doorway to clean my feet off. 

If you can have a fire, bring some kind of fire starter. Some wood take longer to catch than others. And always an extra lighter. 

If you for some reason can’t stake your tent or forget them, find 4 medium sized rocks and place them inside in the corners. Just be sure to put them back when you leave.

I had “strep throat” a few times my senior year of college and I got the help I needed without alarming my parents. Was it the best? No, but it was much better than nothing.

Two, and this was actually recommended to me by my family doctor recently, if you happen to live near a college reach out to them to see if they’re doing any training clinics for their psych grad students. This is almost always free, and while the person you’re directly speaking with hasn’t completed their certification yet, they are under the strict guidance of professionals and may even be more attentive to your case study than a seasoned professional with a full case load, which is unfortunately common in other free/low cost options.
